name: Bereshit
summary: God creates the world in six days and rests on the seventh. Adam and Eve live in Eden, eat the forbidden fruit, and are sent out of the garden. Cain kills Abel. The generations from Adam to Noah are listed; then God sees human wickedness spread, but Noah finds favor.

richContent.narrativeSummary: God creates heaven and earth over six days (light; sky; land and plants; the great lights; creatures of sea and sky; and finally land animals and humankind), then ceases from the work on the seventh day and blesses it, the pattern the Torah later gives as the reason for Shabbat (Exodus 20:11). God places the first human in the garden of Eden and forbids the fruit of the tree of knowledge of good and bad; the serpent persuades the woman, and both eat. They hide, and are sent out of the garden. Outside it, Cain kills his brother Abel after God pays heed to Abel's offering and not to his, and is sent to wander, with a mark from God to protect him. Cain founds a city; among his descendants, Jabal and Jubal are the ancestors of herders and of musicians, and Tubal-cain forges copper and iron (4:17–22). Chapter 5 traces ten generations from Adam to Noah, and the portion closes as God sees human wickedness and regrets having made humankind, but Noah finds favor with God.
richContent.didYouKnow: Rashi notes that the Hebrew word reshit is always joined to what it is the beginning of, so in its plain sense he reads the opening as 'at the beginning of God's creating heaven and earth…', and says the verse is not meant to teach the order in which things were created. The first verse of Genesis has exactly seven Hebrew words; the second has fourteen, counting hyphen-joined words separately.
richContent.historicalContext: Other peoples of the ancient Near East told their own creation stories. The oldest copies of the Babylonian Epic of Atrahasis date to about 1650 BCE, and the Babylonian Enuma Elish is usually dated to around 1100 BCE. In the Enuma Elish, creation follows a battle between gods, and the world is formed from the body of the slain goddess Tiamat. In Atrahasis, people are made from clay mixed with a slain god's flesh and blood, to do the gods' labor. Genesis shares some features with these stories, such as the waters of the deep and the separation of heaven from earth, but differs sharply: one God, no battle, no god dies, humankind is made in God's image, and creation is called 'very good.' Scholars debate how directly Genesis responds to these stories.
richContent.jewishTradition: Rashi opens his Torah commentary by quoting Rabbi Isaac's question: why does the Torah begin with creation rather than with the first commandment given to Israel (Exodus 12:2)? The answer: if the nations call Israel robbers for taking the land of Canaan, Israel can reply that the whole earth belongs to God, who created it and gives it to whom God pleases. Shabbat itself is rooted here: the account's closing verses (Genesis 2:1–3, 'The heaven and the earth were finished…') are said in the Friday-night Kiddush over wine, right after the words 'the sixth day' (1:31).

name: Noach
summary: God floods the earth to wipe out wickedness; Noah builds an ark and survives with his family and pairs of every animal (seven pairs of each pure animal and of the birds). After the waters recede, God makes a covenant never to flood the earth again and sets a rainbow as its sign. Humanity spreads and then unites to build the Tower of Babel, which God scatters.

richContent.narrativeSummary: The earth has become corrupt and filled with lawlessness, and God resolves to put an end to all flesh — save for one righteous man, Noah, whom God instructs to build a massive wooden ark and fill it with his family and every species of animal. The flood comes for forty days and forty nights, submerging even the highest mountains; for one hundred and fifty days the waters dominate the earth until God 'remembers' Noah and sends a wind. When the mountaintops appear, Noah sends out birds to see whether the waters have gone down; once the earth is dry he leaves the ark and offers sacrifices on an altar, and God seals a covenant with all living creatures — symbolized by a rainbow — never to flood the world again. Then comes a second origin story: humanity's descendants unite to build a tower with its top in the sky, and God confounds their speech and scatters them across the earth. The portion closes with the ten generations from Shem to Abram, whose father Terah leaves Ur of the Chaldeans and dies in Haran.
richContent.didYouKnow: Outside the Flood story, the Torah uses the word for 'ark' — tevah — only for the basket that carries the infant Moses on the Nile (Exodus 2:3, 5): both vessels, sealed with pitch, save a life on the water. The flood narrative also contains a precise date system: the waters rose on the seventeenth of the second month and the ark rested on the seventeenth of the seventh month, five months later. With 30-day months that matches the 150 days of 7:24; Rashi (on 8:3) instead counts the 150 days from the end of the forty days of rain.
richContent.historicalContext: Flood narratives appear across ancient Near Eastern literature, most famously in the Epic of Gilgamesh (Tablet XI), where the hero Utnapishtim survives a divine flood on a boat and releases birds — a dove and a swallow, which come back, then a raven, which does not — to find dry land, recalling Noah's raven and dove. The Atrahasis Epic similarly features a flood sent by gods frustrated by human noise. Most scholars think the Genesis account draws on these older Mesopotamian traditions. Some archaeologists have linked the Mesopotamian flood stories to real river floods, such as the one that left a layer of flood deposits at Shuruppak, Utnapishtim's city, around 2900 BCE.
richContent.jewishTradition: The rabbis debated Noah's righteousness sharply: was he truly righteous, or only relatively so — 'in his generations' implying a low bar? The Talmud (Sanhedrin 108a) records that debate between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish, and pictures Noah urging his neighbors to repent while they mocked him (108a–b). Rashi (on 7:7) counts Noah among those 'wanting in faith', who entered the ark only when the waters forced him. The Zohar (3:14b–15a) faults him for not praying for the world, as Moses would for Israel; Abraham, too, will later plead for Sodom (Genesis 18:23–32). The seven Noahide Laws — the basic moral code binding on all humanity according to rabbinic tradition — are named for Noah's descendants: Rabbi Yochanan in the Talmud (Sanhedrin 56b) derives them from God's command to Adam (Genesis 2:16), and the ban on eating flesh with its life-blood is stated to Noah here (9:4).

name: Lech-Lecha
summary: God calls Abram to leave his homeland for Canaan, promising him land, descendants, and blessing. Abram travels through Canaan, sojourns in Egypt, separates from Lot, and rescues him from a war of kings. God seals a covenant with Abram, promising the land. Hagar bears Ishmael. God renames Abram to Abraham, institutes circumcision, and promises a son through Sarai, who becomes Sarah.

richContent.narrativeSummary: God's call to Abram opens with two words, 'lech lecha' (go forth): he is to leave his land, his birthplace and his father's house for a land God will show him. With it comes a promise: God will make of him a great nation, and through him all the families of the earth will be blessed. Abram goes, as God told him (12:4), with his wife Sarai, his nephew Lot and their household, from Haran into Canaan, and then down to Egypt during a famine, where Pharaoh takes Sarai into his palace until God strikes his household with plagues and he sends them away. Back in Canaan, after their herdsmen quarrel, Abram and Lot part ways, and Lot settles near Sodom. When four kings raid the region and carry Lot off, Abram pursues them and rescues him. God makes a covenant with Abram, as a smoking oven and a flaming torch pass between the halves of the animals, promising the land to his descendants. Sarai gives Abram her servant Hagar, who bears Ishmael. Finally God changes Abram's name to Abraham and Sarai's to Sarah, gives circumcision as the sign of the covenant, and promises that Sarah will bear a son at this time next year.
richContent.didYouKnow: Abram (אַבְרָם) becomes Abraham (אַבְרָהָם) with one added letter, hei; the verse explains the new name: 'I make you the father of a multitude of nations' (17:5). The Talmud (Berakhot 13a) reads the old name as 'father of Aram'. Sarai (שָׂרַי) becomes Sarah (שָׂרָה) when her last letter, yud, is replaced by a hei. In a midrash (Bereshit Rabbah 47:1), Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha says the yud taken from Sarai was divided, half for Sarah and half for Abraham. The midrash doesn't spell out the math, but the usual explanation is numerical: yud is worth 10, and hei, the letter each of them received, is worth 5.
richContent.historicalContext: No one knows when Abram lived. Scholars who try to date him usually place him in the Middle Bronze Age (c. 2000–1550 BCE), but most scholars today doubt the stories can be tied to any period, and many think they were written down centuries later. Traditional Jewish chronology, counting the years in Genesis, puts Abram's departure from Haran around 1738 BCE. In the early part of that age, Egypt was a strong, united kingdom under its 12th Dynasty, Amorite kingdoms ruled much of Mesopotamia and Syria, and walled cities were being built again in Canaan. By about 1738 BCE, the 13th Dynasty had taken over from the 12th in Egypt. A childless wife giving her husband a servant to bear a child for her, as Sarai does with Hagar, appears in texts from across the ancient Near East: an Old Assyrian marriage contract (c. 1900 BCE), Hammurabi's laws (c. 1750 BCE) and later Nuzi tablets. Because the custom lasted so long, scholars no longer use it to date the stories.
richContent.jewishTradition: The Mishnah (Avot 5:3) says Abraham was tested ten times and withstood them all. In Maimonides' list (Commentary on the Mishnah, Avot 5:3), six of the ten come in this portion, starting with 'go forth from your land' and including the famine, Sarai taken to Pharaoh, the war with the four kings, Hagar and circumcision; the tenth is the binding of Isaac, later in Genesis. Circumcision (brit milah), given here as the sign of the covenant, is done on the eighth day (17:12), later if the baby is unwell. Maimonides (Guide for the Perplexed 3:49) explains the eighth day: in their first seven days newborns are very weak, 'as if they were still in the womb of their mother'.

name: Vayera
summary: Three visitors (angels, in tradition) come to Abraham and promise that Sarah will bear a son. Abraham pleads with God to spare Sodom; the city and Gomorrah are destroyed for their wickedness but Lot escapes. Isaac is born to Abraham and Sarah. Hagar and Ishmael are sent away. God tests Abraham by commanding him to sacrifice Isaac — at the last moment an angel stops him.

richContent.narrativeSummary: Three mysterious visitors appear at Abraham's tent in the heat of the day; Abraham rushes to welcome them with a meal of cakes of choice flour, a tender calf, curds and milk, and one announces that Sarah — listening at the tent entrance and laughing to herself — will have a son within a year. The visitors then turn toward Sodom, and God tells Abraham of the outcry against Sodom and Gomorrah; Abraham launches into an extraordinary moral negotiation, pressing God to spare the city if even ten righteous people can be found there. Angels lead Lot, his wife and his daughters out of Sodom, and Sodom and Gomorrah are destroyed; Lot's wife looks back and becomes a pillar of salt. Sarah indeed gives birth to Isaac, and the household erupts in tension: Sarah demands that Abraham expel Hagar and Ishmael, and though Abraham is grieved, God tells him to listen to Sarah, promising to make a nation of Ishmael too. The portion culminates in the Akedah — the binding of Isaac — where God commands Abraham to offer his son on a height in the land of Moriah; Abraham rises early, sees the place from afar on the third day, and takes up the knife before an angel stops him: 'now I know that you fear God.'
richContent.didYouKnow: In Abraham's negotiation with God over Sodom — arguing down from fifty righteous people to ten — a human being bargains with the Creator over the terms of justice. Why stop at ten? Rashi (citing Genesis Rabbah 49:13) explains that Noah's family of eight had not been enough to save their generation from the Flood. The Akedah takes place in 'the land of Moriah'; 2 Chronicles 3:1 places Solomon's Temple 'on Mount Moriah', and tradition identifies the site with the Temple Mount in Jerusalem.
richContent.historicalContext: Where Sodom stood is unknown. Genesis places the cities of the Plain near the Jordan and the Dead Sea (13:10; 14:3). One theory looks south, to the Early Bronze Age towns of Bab edh-Dhra and Numeira by the Dead Sea; another looks north, to Tall el-Hammam in the Jordan Valley, a large Middle Bronze Age city. A 2021 study claiming that a cosmic airburst destroyed Tall el-Hammam was retracted in 2025, and neither theory has won general acceptance.
richContent.jewishTradition: The Akedah (binding of Isaac) is the Torah reading for the second day of Rosh Hashana — and the ram's-horn shofar blown on Rosh Hashana recalls the ram caught in the thicket and offered in Isaac's place (Talmud, Rosh Hashanah 16a). The liturgy of Rosh Hashana invokes the 'merit of the Akedah' repeatedly, asking God to remember Abraham's willingness and show mercy to his descendants. The visit of the three guests, with Abraham offering lavish hospitality to strangers, is the classic biblical source for the commandment of hachnasat orchim — welcoming guests; the Talmud (Shabbat 127a) learns from it that welcoming guests is greater than receiving the Divine Presence.

name: Chayei Sarah
summary: Sarah dies and Abraham buys the Cave of Machpelah in Hebron as a burial site. Abraham sends his servant to find a wife for Isaac from among his own kin; the servant returns with Rebekah, and Isaac loves her. Abraham dies and is buried with Sarah.

richContent.narrativeSummary: Sarah dies at 127 years old in Hebron — the first time the Torah tells of anyone mourning and weeping for the dead — and Abraham negotiates carefully with the Hittites to purchase the Cave of Machpelah as a permanent burial site, paying the full price in silver: the first purchase of land the Torah tells of. Abraham then sends his senior servant, who had charge of all he owned, on a mission to Aram-naharaim, in northern Mesopotamia, to find a wife for Isaac from his own family, making him swear not to choose a Canaanite woman; the servant, guided by a prayer at a well, sees Rebekah appear before he has finished praying — and she does just what he prayed for. Rebekah agrees to leave her family immediately and travel to marry a man she has never met; Isaac, out in the field toward evening, sees the camels approaching, and when she arrives he brings her into his mother's tent and loves her — the first time the Torah uses the word 'love' for a marriage. Abraham remarries, fathers six more sons, and dies at 175; both Isaac and Ishmael bury him with Sarah in the Cave of Machpelah.
richContent.didYouKnow: The enclosure over the Cave of Machpelah in Hebron, built by Herod the Great, is the only fully surviving Herodian building, and it is still used for prayer today. The parsha takes its name, 'Chayei Sarah' (the life of Sarah), from its opening words, yet the portion opens with her death, and she never appears alive in the portion named for her. The servant's prayer at the well — asking that the right girl offer water to him and to his camels — is answered before he has finished speaking (24:15).
richContent.historicalContext: The purchase reads like a formal legal record: a public negotiation before the assembly at the town gate, a price of silver 'at the going merchants' rate', and a list of what passes with the land — the field, its cave and all its trees (23:16–18). Scholars once linked it to Hittite law; later scholars compared it instead to the 'dialogue' sale documents known especially from Neo-Babylonian times (first millennium BCE). Who these Hittites of Hebron were is uncertain.
richContent.jewishTradition: The Cave of Machpelah became the family burial site of the patriarchs and three of the four matriarchs: the Torah says Abraham and Sarah, Isaac and Rebekah, and Jacob and Leah were buried there (49:31; 50:13), while Rachel was buried on the road to Ephrath (35:19). It remains one of Judaism's holiest sites, though access has been deeply contested: for centuries, until 1967, Jews were barred from the building and could go no higher than the seventh step outside. The servant's mission is told twice — once as it happens and again at length in his own retelling — and Rashi quotes Rabbi Acha (Genesis Rabbah 60:8): the ordinary conversation of the patriarchs' servants is more pleasing to God than even the Torah of their descendants.

name: Toldot
summary: Rebekah gives birth to the twins Esau and Jacob after a difficult pregnancy. Esau, the elder, sells his birthright to Jacob for a bowl of stew. Isaac settles among the Philistines and prospers. Rebekah helps Jacob disguise himself to steal Esau's blessing from a blind Isaac, and Jacob flees to Haran before Esau can take revenge.

richContent.narrativeSummary: Rebekah is pregnant with twins who struggle in her womb; she asks 'If so, why do I exist?' and goes to inquire of God, and is told that two nations are in her womb and that the older shall serve the younger (25:23). Esau emerges first, red and hairy, followed by Jacob grasping Esau's heel; they grow into opposite types, Esau the outdoor hunter beloved by Isaac, Jacob the quiet tent-dweller favored by Rebekah. The first recorded negotiation between them is also the most consequential: Esau returns famished from the field and sells his birthright, his rights as firstborn, to Jacob for bread and a red lentil stew (25:30, 25:34), swearing an oath and walking away. The portion's climax is the elaborate deception of the blessing: Rebekah dresses Jacob in Esau's best clothes and covers his hands and neck with the skins of young goats, and Isaac, whose eyes are too dim to see, hears Jacob's voice but feels hairy hands (27:22–23) and pronounces on Jacob a blessing of abundance, dominion, and nations bowing before him. When Esau arrives moments later, Isaac lets the blessing stand ('now he must remain blessed!' 27:33), and Esau, learning what has happened, weeps.
richContent.didYouKnow: The Torah connects the name Jacob (Ya'akov, יַעֲקֹב) with akev, 'heel' (25:26), and Esau puns on it bitterly when Jacob takes his blessing: 'Was he, then, named Jacob that he might supplant me these two times?' (27:36). Rashi on 27:19 reads Jacob's words 'I am Esau, your first-born' as two statements, 'I am he that brings food to you, and Esau is your first-born', and on 27:24 notes that Jacob answers only 'I am', not 'I am Esau'. The Torah traces the Edomites to Esau (36:9), and rabbinic sources identify Edom with Rome: the Talmud (Megillah 6a) calls the Roman city of Caesarea 'daughter of Edom'.
richContent.historicalContext: The Torah itself gives the firstborn (bekhor) a double share of the inheritance (Deuteronomy 21:17). A tablet from Nuzi in Mesopotamia (15th century BCE) records a man giving up his inheritance share of a grove to his brother in exchange for three sheep; it was once taken as a birthright sale like Esau's, though nothing in it shows that a firstborn's rights were at stake. In the story itself, Isaac lets the spoken blessing stand: 'I blessed him; now he must remain blessed!' (27:33); Rashi reads this as Isaac confirming it of his own free will.
richContent.jewishTradition: The struggle between Jacob and Esau generated one of the richest traditions in rabbinic literature, particularly the identification of Esau/Edom with Rome. The Talmud (Megillah 6a, quoted by Rashi on 25:23) reads 'one people shall be stronger than the other' to mean that the two will never be great at the same time: when one rises, the other falls. Esau's plea for 'that red stuff' — the lentil stew for which he sold his birthright — is why he was named Edom, 'red' (25:30).

name: Vayetze
summary: Jacob sets out for Haran and on the way dreams of a stairway reaching to the sky, with angels going up and down on it. At a well he meets Rachel, and he works seven years for her in Laban's house, but Laban gives him Leah first. A week later he marries Rachel too, for another seven years of work. Eleven sons and a daughter are born to him. After twenty years, grown rich in flocks (God's doing, he tells his wives, 31:9), Jacob leaves secretly with his family for Canaan.

richContent.narrativeSummary: Jacob flees his brother's murderous anger. Stopping for the night, he puts a stone under his head and dreams of a stairway, or ladder, reaching from earth to the sky, with angels going up and down on it, while God stands beside him (Rashi reads: above him) and promises him the land, descendants like the dust of the earth, and protection wherever he goes (28:13–15). In the land of the Easterners he comes to a well whose shepherds are from Haran. When Rachel arrives with her father's flock, he rolls the stone off the well by himself (Rashi, from Bereshit Rabbah 70:12, sees great strength in this), waters the flock, kisses her and weeps, and tells her he is her father's kinsman; Laban runs to greet him and takes him home. Laban deceives Jacob: Jacob works seven years for Rachel, which 'seemed to him but a few days because of his love for her,' but after the wedding feast Laban brings Leah to him instead, and Jacob discovers the switch only in the morning. A week later he marries Rachel too, for seven more years of work, and eleven sons and a daughter, Dinah, are born amid a painful rivalry between the two sisters, who each also give Jacob her maid. After fourteen years Jacob agrees with Laban to take the speckled and spotted animals as his wages; over six more years, though Laban changes his wages time and again, he grows very wealthy (God's doing, he tells his wives, 31:9), and after twenty years in all he flees secretly toward home.
richContent.didYouKnow: The seven years Jacob worked for Rachel are described in one short sentence: 'they seemed to him but a few days because of his love for her' (Genesis 29:20). Eleven of the twelve sons whose descendants become the tribes of Israel are born in this portion, to four different mothers; the twelfth, Benjamin, is born in the next. The name Israel isn't given until the next portion, so these sons are born to a man still called Jacob, far from home.
richContent.historicalContext: Scholars once explained Jacob's years with Laban through adoption contracts of the Nuzi type from northern Mesopotamia (15th–14th centuries BCE, later than the Middle Bronze Age where these stories are often placed), in which a man adopted a son-in-law as his heir. The idea rests largely on a single tablet (Gadd 51, found at nearby Arrapha), and most scholars no longer accept it. The same tablets were used to explain why Rachel steals her father's teraphim (JPS: "oracle idols"; Laban calls them "my gods," 31:30), as a claim to his inheritance, but other Nuzi texts show that holding such figurines did not by itself give such a claim, and the Torah never says why she took them.
richContent.jewishTradition: Jacob's dream of the ladder has been read in many ways. In the Midrash (Leviticus Rabbah 29:2), Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥman sees the angels as the guardian angels of the kingdoms that would rule over Israel (Babylon, Media, Greece and Edom, which the Rabbis identified with Rome) climbing the ladder. The Talmud (Chullin 91b) teaches that the angels went up to gaze at Jacob's image above and came down to gaze at him below; the Targum attributed to Jonathan (on 28:12) says that image was set in the Throne of Glory. According to one teaching in the Talmud (Berakhot 26b, following Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Ḥanina), Abraham instituted the morning prayer, Isaac the afternoon prayer, and Jacob, here, as night falls, the evening prayer.

name: Vayishlach
summary: Jacob prepares anxiously to meet his brother Esau, and wrestles through the night with a being who renames him Israel. The brothers meet in peace. Jacob's daughter Dinah is violated in Shechem, and her brothers Simeon and Levi take violent revenge. At Bethel God gives him the name Israel again. Rachel dies giving birth to Benjamin. Jacob comes to his father Isaac at Hebron, and Isaac dies.

richContent.narrativeSummary: After twenty years in Laban's house, Jacob must face Esau, who had resolved to kill him after Jacob took their father's blessing (27:41), and his messengers return to report that Esau is coming with four hundred men. Greatly frightened, Jacob divides his camp, prays for rescue, and sends droves of gifts ahead. That night he takes his family across the ford of the Jabbok and, left alone, wrestles until dawn with a mysterious being who cannot defeat him but wrenches his hip; the being renames him Israel, 'for you have striven with beings divine and human, and have prevailed' (32:29), and Jacob names the place Peniel. When they meet, Esau runs to him and the brothers embrace and weep (33:4); then they part, Esau back to Seir, Jacob on to Succoth and then Shechem. There his daughter Dinah goes out to visit the daughters of the land and is seized and violated by Shechem son of Hamor the Hivite, chief of the country, who then wants to marry her. Jacob's sons answer with guile, demanding that every male be circumcised, and on the third day, while the men are in pain, Simeon and Levi kill all the males and their brothers plunder the city; Jacob rebukes them: 'You have brought trouble on me' (34:30). At Bethel God gives him the name Israel again (35:10). On the road to Ephrath, now Bethlehem, Rachel dies in childbirth, naming her last son Ben-oni (understood as 'son of my suffering,' or 'strength') before Jacob names him Benjamin; and Isaac dies at 180, buried by both his sons, before a closing list of Esau's descendants, the Edomites.
keyFigures: The man who wrestled with Jacob
richContent.didYouKnow: The name Israel, given the night Jacob took his family across the ford of the Jabbok (32:23–29) and again at Bethel (35:10), becomes the name of an entire nation. The Torah explains the name itself: 'you have striven with beings divine and human, and have prevailed' (32:29); some modern scholars read it instead as 'El will rule.' The Torah never names the one Jacob wrestled with: it calls him 'a man,' though Jacob says afterward, 'I have seen a divine being face to face' (32:31); Hosea 12:5 says it was an angel, and the Midrash (Genesis Rabbah 77:3, quoted by Rashi) says it was Esau's guardian angel. The ban on eating the gid hanasheh (the sinew at the hip socket, traditionally identified as the sciatic nerve) is tied to this episode: the Torah says Israel does not eat it 'since Jacob's hip socket was wrenched' (32:33).
richContent.historicalContext: The Torah sets Jacob's wrestling on the night he took his family across the ford of the Jabbok (32:23–25), today's Zarqa River in Jordan, which cuts through the hills of Gilead down to the Jordan; in the Bible it marks the border of the Ammonites (Deuteronomy 3:16). The city of Shechem (Tell Balata, beside modern Nablus) was one of the most important Bronze Age cities in Canaan; from about 1900 BCE it was a major political and religious center for much of the second millennium BCE. It appears in Egyptian sources: a 19th-century BCE stela of the officer Khu-Sebek records a campaign in which 'Sekmem', usually identified with Shechem, fell, and, centuries later, the 14th-century BCE Amarna letters include letters from Labaya, ruler of Shechem.
richContent.jewishTradition: The name given the night Jacob took his family across the ford of the Jabbok, Israel, 'for you have striven with beings divine and human, and have prevailed' (32:29), and given again at Bethel (35:10), became the name of the whole people. The ban on eating the gid hanasheh (traditionally identified as the sciatic nerve) is written here (32:33). In the Mishnah (Chullin 7:6), the Rabbis say it was given at Sinai and recorded at this point in the story, while Rabbi Yehuda holds that Jacob's sons already kept it.

name: Vayeshev
summary: Jacob loves Joseph best of all his sons and makes him an ornamented tunic; his brothers hate him, and after his dreams they hate him even more. They throw Joseph into a pit, and he is sold to a caravan heading to Egypt; the brothers deceive their father into thinking he is dead. The narrative then turns to Judah and Tamar. In Egypt, Joseph serves in Potiphar's house but is falsely accused and imprisoned. In prison, Joseph correctly interprets the dreams of Pharaoh's cupbearer and baker.

richContent.narrativeSummary: Joseph is seventeen, the child of Jacob's old age, whom his father loves best of all his sons, and his father has made him an ornamented tunic (the Hebrew's meaning is uncertain). Seeing that their father loves him more than any of them, his brothers hate him so that they cannot speak a friendly word to him (37:4); Joseph also brings bad reports of them to their father. When he tells his dream of their sheaves bowing to his sheaf, they hate him even more (37:8), and when he tells of the sun, the moon and eleven stars bowing to him, they are wrought up at him (37:11). When Joseph finds his brothers at Dothan, they strip him of his tunic and throw him into a pit (it was empty, the Torah notes, with no water in it), then sit down to a meal; he is sold for twenty pieces of silver (the verses name both a caravan of Ishmaelites and passing Midianite traders), and they dip his tunic in the blood of a kid and have it taken to their father, who concludes that a savage beast has devoured him. The narrative then turns to Judah. He marries the daughter of a Canaanite named Shua; his son Er marries Tamar and dies, and the next son, Onan, told to do his duty by her as a brother-in-law, dies too. Judah sends Tamar home to wait for his third son, Shelah, but does not give him to her. Tamar, her face veiled, waits by the road to Timnah and becomes pregnant by Judah, who does not recognize her; when he orders her burned, she produces his seal, cord and staff, and he says, 'She is more in the right than I' (38:26). In Egypt, GOD is with Joseph and he prospers in Potiphar's house, until Potiphar's wife, whom he refuses, accuses him falsely. He is imprisoned, and there, telling them 'Surely God can interpret!' (40:8), he correctly interprets the dreams of Pharaoh's imprisoned cupbearer and baker; the cupbearer, restored to his post, forgets him.
richContent.didYouKnow: The Greek Septuagint calls it a many-colored (poikilos) tunic, and the King James Version's 'coat of many colours' gives the same sense; the meaning of the Hebrew ketonet passim is uncertain. name: Miketz

Scholars have proposed Egyptian readings of the name Pharaoh gives him, Zaphenath-paneah, such as 'the god speaks and he lives' (Georg Steindorff, 1889; the JPS note gives 'God speaks; he lives,' or 'creator of life'), but none is certain; the Aramaic Targum Onkelos renders it 'the man to whom hidden things are revealed.' A much later Egyptian text, the Famine Stela on Sehel Island near Aswan (carved in the Ptolemaic period), tells of seven years of low Nile under King Djoser; seven years of famine is a motif known from Egyptian, Akkadian and Canaanite literature. Josephus already connected the Hyksos, rulers probably of Levantine origin who governed Lower Egypt c. 1650–1550 BCE, with the Israelites, and some modern writers set Joseph's rise in that period; historians do not agree on a setting, and many scholars read the Joseph story as a literary work that took its present form centuries later.

name: Vayigash
summary: Judah steps forward and pleads for Benjamin, offering to stay as a slave in his place. Then Judah steps forward and makes a long plea, recounting their father's grief and his own pledge to bring Benjamin back, and offering himself as a slave in Benjamin's place so that their father will not die of grief: 'For how can I go back to my father unless the boy is with me?' 'I am Joseph,' he says. 'Is my father still well?' The brothers are too dumfounded to answer. 'It was to save life that God sent me ahead of you,' he tells them (45:5), and later, 'it is indeed I who am speaking to you' (45:12): in Hebrew, Rashi explains. He embraces Benjamin, kisses all his brothers, and sends them back to bring Jacob. In the Tosefta (Berakhot 4:16; 4:16–18 in Lieberman's edition), Rabbi Tarfon asks his students why Judah merited kingship, and the passage, which also tells of four elders discussing the question, weighs several answers. One is his humility in this very speech: 'please let your servant remain as a slave to my lord instead of the boy' (44:33). It is turned down, because Judah had pledged himself as surety for Benjamin (44:32), and a surety must in the end make good his pledge. The answer the passage ends with is that Judah's tribe went down into the sea first and sanctified God's name. A New Kingdom frontier report (Papyrus Anastasi VI, late 13th century BCE, dated to the reign of Merneptah or of Seti II) records Shasu (nomad) tribes from Edom being admitted at a fortress in Tjeku, in the Wadi Tumilat, to the lakes of Per-Atum 'to keep them alive and to keep their flocks alive' (as Bietak and Rendsburg quote it). Most scholars, they write, see this as an exceedingly close parallel to the biblical story, where the brothers ask to stay in Goshen because there is no pasture for their flocks (47:4). Joseph's role, second only to Pharaoh (41:40), is often compared to the Egyptian vizier (tjaty); one 14th-century BCE vizier, Aper-el, bore a name that Alain Zivie, who excavated his tomb, reads as Semitic: 'Abdi-El, 'servant of El'. Both come from Egypt's New Kingdom, later than the Middle Bronze Age (c. 2000–1550 BCE) where some place these stories; they show the kind of world the story describes, not a date for it. Historians do not agree whether the Joseph story reflects real events, and many scholars read it as a literary work written down centuries later.

name: Vayechi
summary: Jacob lives in Egypt for seventeen years. When he falls ill, he blesses Joseph's two sons, Ephraim and Manasseh, putting the younger first. When his brothers fear that Joseph will pay them back, Joseph reassures them that he will sustain them. Joseph dies at 110, making the sons of Israel swear that, when God takes notice of them, they will carry his bones up from Egypt.

When Joseph is told that his father is ill, he comes with his two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim, and Jacob asks to bless them. Jacob crosses his hands to lay his right hand on the younger, Ephraim, and when Joseph objects, he answers, 'I know, my son, I know.' He then gathers all twelve sons to tell them 'what is to befall you in days to come' (49:1), with a parting word for each (49:28), often in vivid images: Reuben 'unstable as water', Simeon and Levi, whose 'weapons are tools of lawlessness', Judah 'a lion's whelp' from whom 'the scepter shall not depart', Joseph 'a wild ass' in the JPS translation (others translate 'a fruitful bough'), Benjamin 'a ravenous wolf'. Jacob dies at 147, and a very large company, including Pharaoh's officials, Egypt's dignitaries, and chariots and charioteers, goes up with Joseph and his brothers to bury him in Canaan (50:7–9). After the burial, back in Egypt, the brothers fear that Joseph still bears a grudge against them (50:14–15); Joseph is in tears as they speak, then replies: 'although you intended me harm, God intended it for good' (50:20). The blessing of Judah, 'The scepter shall not depart from Judah, Nor the ruler's staff from between his feet' (49:10), goes on in words whose meaning is uncertain: JPS reads them 'so that tribute shall come to him', following the Midrash; literally they say 'until he comes to Shiloh'; Onkelos and Rashi read 'until the Messiah comes'. It became a much-debated verse in Jewish and Christian interpretation. Joseph's request that his bones be carried up from Egypt is fulfilled generations later, when Moses takes Joseph's bones with him out of Egypt (Exodus 13:19).
richContent.historicalContext: The Torah says the physicians in Joseph's service embalmed Jacob, taking forty days, and that the Egyptians bewailed him seventy days (50:2–3), close to the seventy-two days of mourning that the Greek historian Diodorus, writing in the 1st century BCE, says all Egypt observed for a king. Egyptians were preserving the dead by the early dynasties (about 2800 BCE). New Kingdom tomb paintings (from about 1550 BCE), such as the vizier Ramose's at Thebes, show funeral processions, and many mummies survive, but the embalming procedure itself is described mainly by the later Greek writers Herodotus and Diodorus. Egypt had long trade and political ties with Canaan, and under the New Kingdom (c. 1550–1070 BCE) Canaan came under Egyptian control, governed mostly through local vassal rulers, with Egyptian garrisons and officials. The New Kingdom evidence is later than the Middle Bronze Age (c. 2000–1550 BCE) where some place these stories, and Diodorus later still.

Jacob's blessing 'God make you like Ephraim and Manasseh' (48:20) is spoken by many Jewish parents over their sons on Friday night.

name: Shemot
summary: A new Pharaoh who doesn't know Joseph enslaves the Israelites and orders their infant boys drowned. Moses is born, hidden in a basket on the Nile, rescued by Pharaoh's daughter, and raised in the palace. He kills an Egyptian beating a Hebrew, flees to Midian, and marries. The response is systematic oppression — forced labor building the store cities of Pithom and Raamses — then a secret order to the Hebrew midwives to kill every newborn boy, which the midwives subvert by fearing God more than Pharaoh. Into this world Moses is born, hidden three months, then placed in a waterproofed basket among the Nile reeds where Pharaoh's own daughter finds him, takes pity, and his sister arranges for his own mother to be his wet-nurse. Moses grows up in the palace but his identity stays with him: he sees an Egyptian beating a Hebrew, looks both ways, and kills the Egyptian; when his deed becomes known he flees to Midian where he meets Jethro's daughters at a well, defends them from local bullies, and marries Zipporah. Then, tending his father-in-law's flock near Mount Horeb, Moses sees a bush burning without being consumed — and from it God calls his name twice, tells him the divine name YHWH, and charges Moses with the impossible task: go to Pharaoh and bring my people out of Egypt.

The divine name revealed at the burning bush — YHWH — is so sacred in Jewish tradition that it is never pronounced as written; Jews substitute 'Adonai' (my Lord) in prayer and 'Hashem' (the Name) in everyday speech.
richContent.historicalContext: Of the two store cities the Israelites were forced to build, Raamses is usually identified with Pi-Ramesses, the capital built by Ramesses II (r. 1279–1213 BCE) in the eastern Nile Delta, and excavations have uncovered its enormous scale. Pithom's location is still debated between two sites, Tell el-Retaba and Tell el-Maskhuta. Egyptian records do mention 'Apiru laborers at Pi-Ramesses: Papyrus Leiden 348 orders grain for soldiers and for 'Apiru 'who are drawing stone for the great pylon.' Early scholars equated the word 'Apiru with 'Hebrew,' but most now see the connection as indirect.
richContent.jewishTradition: Moses is the most important human figure in the Torah, yet the Passover Haggadah names him only once, inside a quoted verse (Exodus 14:31); instead it stresses that God took Israel out of Egypt 'not through an angel, not through a seraph, not through any emissary.' The burning bush that burns without being consumed is read as a symbol of the Jewish people: persecuted but never destroyed. God calling Moses's name twice ('Moses! Moses!') is one of three such double calls in the Torah, with Abraham and Jacob (a fourth, Samuel, is in the Prophets); the Midrash (Shemot Rabbah 2:6) reads the doubling as an expression of fondness and encouragement.

name: Vaera
summary: God reaffirms the covenant with Moses and Aaron and sends them to Pharaoh. When Pharaoh refuses to let the Israelites go, God unleashes the first seven plagues upon Egypt: water turning to blood, frogs, lice, wild animals, livestock disease, boils, and devastating hail — each time Pharaoh's heart is hardened and he refuses.

The Israelites' groaning under slavery has reached God, and the liberation is about to begin — but Moses faces immediate failure. When he and Aaron return to Pharaoh, the court magicians match Aaron's staff-into-serpent sign (though Aaron's serpent swallows theirs), and Pharaoh dismisses them. Then the plagues begin in earnest, and as the commentator Rashbam notes, they come in sets of three: Pharaoh is warned before the first two plagues of each set, and the third comes without warning. This portion covers the first two sets and the first plague of the third. The Nile runs red with blood for seven days; then frogs surge out of every body of water and invade every room of every home; then lice emerge from the dust and even the Egyptian magicians concede these are the finger of God. Wild beasts swarm, Egyptian livestock die of disease, boils afflict every Egyptian body — and each time, once the immediate suffering eases, Pharaoh's heart hardens. The seventh plague, hail mixed with fire, devastates Egypt's crops and breaks the hardest heart momentarily — until the storm stops.

The Ipuwer Papyrus, an Egyptian document of uncertain date, describes a period of chaos including rivers of blood, death, and social collapse — tantalizing but too vaguely dated to confirm any connection.
richContent.historicalContext: The Late Bronze Age (c. 1550–1200 BCE) corresponds to the period the Exodus narrative depicts. Egypt was at the height of its imperial power under the New Kingdom pharaohs, controlling Canaan through a network of garrisons and vassal city-states. The identification of the Exodus Pharaoh remains debated: Ramesses II (r. 1279–1213 BCE) is the most popular candidate due to his building projects in the Delta and the timing, though some scholars favor earlier rulers or see the narrative as composite tradition rather than a single historical event.

Maimonides (Laws of Repentance 6:3) argues that God's hardening of Pharaoh's heart was itself a punishment: Pharaoh had first sinned by his own free will, so justice required that he be kept from repenting. Rashi (on 7:3) adds that for the first five plagues the Torah says only that Pharaoh's heart was hardened, not that God hardened it. At the Passover seder, a drop of wine is removed from the cup for each of the ten plagues (the Rema, Orach Chayim 473:7, records sixteen drops in all, adding related words); a popular explanation is that our joy cannot be complete while others suffered, even enemies who oppressed us.

name: Bo
summary: The last three plagues strike Egypt: locusts devour the land, darkness covers it for three days, and finally the firstborn of every Egyptian family dies at midnight. richContent.historicalContext: No Egyptian record names the biblical Exodus. Some scholars think the story may preserve memories of the expulsion of the Hyksos, rulers of probable Semitic origin who governed northern Egypt from their capital Avaris until they were driven out about 1550 BCE.
richContent.jewishTradition: The Passover seder is one of the most widely observed Jewish rituals: a structured retelling of this night, with the Haggadah as its script. The commandment appears here with an unusual insistence on active participation: 'you shall tell your child on that day.' The seder's bitter herbs recall the bitterness of slavery, the charoset recalls the mortar used in building, the reclining recalls freedom, and the Jerusalem Talmud (Pesachim 10:1) links the four cups of wine to the four expressions of redemption in Exodus 6:6-7. name: Beshalach
summary: Pharaoh changes his mind and pursues the Israelites with his army. God splits the Sea of Reeds, the Israelites cross on dry land, and the Egyptian army drowns as the waters return. Moses and Miriam lead the people in song. In the desert, the people complain about hunger and thirst; God provides manna, quail, and water from a rock. The Israelites fight and defeat the tribe of Amalek.

The people panic and bitterly wish they had died in Egypt; Moses tells them to stand firm and watch — and God commands Moses to raise his staff over the sea. A great east wind blows all night, the waters split into walls on either side, and the Israelites walk through on dry ground while the pillar of cloud moves behind them to obstruct the Egyptians. When the Egyptians follow into the seabed, Moses raises his staff again and the waters crash back, drowning the entire army; the Torah notes that Egypt's horses, chariots, and chariot drivers are swept into the sea while Israel looks on from the other shore. Moses bursts into song — the Song of the Sea, whose archaic Hebrew leads some scholars to consider it the oldest surviving account of the Exodus — and Miriam, his sister, leads the women in dance with timbrels. Three days into the wilderness, the water is bitter; then God provides manna from heaven each morning (double on Fridays for Shabbat), quail in the evening, and water from a struck rock. The portion ends with the first military battle: Amalek attacks, and Joshua leads the army while Moses holds his arms up on a hill — when his arms are raised Israel prevails, when they fall Amalek gains.
richContent.didYouKnow: The Song of the Sea (Shirat HaYam) is written in the Torah scroll in a special staggered layout the Talmud (Megillah 16b) calls 'a half brick upon a whole brick', and it is one of the few passages in the Torah whose layout on the page is prescribed. The word 'Shabbat' appears for the first time in this portion in the context of the manna, which did not fall on the seventh day — the Sabbath law is thus embedded in the daily experience of wilderness life before it is formally commanded at Sinai.
richContent.historicalContext: The 'Sea of Reeds' (Yam Suf) is widely discussed archaeologically; the Greek translation 'Red Sea' may be a mistranslation, and various proposed sites along the eastern Delta's network of lakes and marshy areas have been proposed. Military records from the Late Bronze Age show Egyptian chariot forces as the dominant military technology of the period, making their destruction in a body of water a strikingly specific kind of catastrophe. Egyptian texts rarely record military defeats, which may explain why no pharaonic record of this event has been found.
richContent.jewishTradition: The Song of the Sea is recited every morning in the Shacharit prayer service, so observant Jews say it every day of the year. The Talmud (Sotah 30b) records Rabbi Meir's teaching that even babies still in their mothers' wombs sang the song at the Sea. Miriam's brief leadership of the women in song is noted by feminist theologians as one of the rare glimpses of women's liturgical leadership in the biblical text.

The people arrive at Sinai and God instructs them to consecrate themselves, wash their clothes, and be ready on the third day, when the divine presence will descend publicly on the mountain. The theophany is overwhelming: thunder, lightning, thick cloud, a trumpet blast growing louder and louder, the mountain smoking as in a furnace, the entire people trembling. Then God speaks directly to all Israel — the only moment in the Torah where God's voice addresses the whole nation at once — proclaiming the Ten Commandments: one God, no idols, don't misuse the divine name, keep Shabbat, honor your parents, don't murder, commit adultery, steal, bear false witness, or covet.
richContent.didYouKnow: The Ten Commandments appear twice in the Torah, here in Exodus 20 and again in Deuteronomy 5, with several differences; the best known is that Exodus says to 'remember' (zachor) the Sabbath, while Deuteronomy says to 'guard' (shamor) it. The Talmud (Rosh Hashanah 27a) teaches that God spoke both words in a single utterance, 'something that the human mouth cannot speak and the human ear cannot hear', and the Friday night hymn Lecha Dodi repeats this: 'Shamor and zachor in a single utterance.' The number ten is significant: the rabbis connect the Ten Commandments to the ten statements by which God created the world in Genesis, framing revelation as a second creation.
richContent.historicalContext: The Sinai theophany — thunder, lightning, thick smoke, a trembling mountain, divine speech — uses the imagery of a thunderstorm and volcanic activity that appears in other ancient Near Eastern descriptions of divine appearances (theophanies). The Ugaritic texts describe the storm-god Baal in similar terms, thundering and flashing his lightning. Sinai itself has been proposed at many locations in the peninsula and beyond; the traditional site, Jebel Musa in the southern Sinai Peninsula, has drawn pilgrims since at least the 4th century CE, and St. Catherine's Monastery has stood at its foot since the 6th century CE.
richContent.jewishTradition: The giving of the Torah at Sinai is the central event of the Jewish calendar, celebrated each year at Shavuot — fifty days after Passover — when Jews traditionally stay up all night studying Torah. The Talmud (Shabbat 88a) records the striking teaching that the Israelites stood 'beneath the mountain' at Sinai — which the rabbis read as God holding the mountain over their heads as a threat: accept the Torah or be crushed here. Jethro's role is celebrated: the portion that contains the Ten Commandments is named after him, a Midianite priest, and with Noach and Balak it is one of the few portions named after someone outside Israel.

name: Mishpatim
summary: Following the Ten Commandments, God gives Israel a detailed body of civil and social law covering slavery, personal injury, property disputes, obligations to the poor, Sabbath rest, and the three pilgrimage festivals. The people declare "we will do and we will hear," ratifying the covenant. Moses and the elders ascend the mountain and see God; Moses goes up alone for forty days to receive the stone tablets.

richContent.narrativeSummary: Immediately after the Ten Commandments, God begins legislating the details of daily life — demonstrating that revelation and law are inseparable in the Torah. The laws cascade across nearly every domain of ancient society: a Hebrew slave must go free after six years; a deliberate killer is put to death, while someone who kills by accident may flee to a place of refuge; if a thief cannot repay, he may be sold; an ox that gores a person to death must be stoned; if a man seduces a virgin, he must pay the bride price and marry her unless her father refuses. Care for the vulnerable is commanded with unusual force: do not oppress the stranger for you were strangers in Egypt; do not mistreat a widow or orphan; if you take a neighbor's cloak as a pledge, return it before sunset; do not take bribes for bribes blind the clear-sighted. The covenant is ratified in a ceremony of remarkable intimacy: Moses reads the Book of the Covenant to all the people, who respond 'we will do and we will hear' — act before understanding — while Moses sprinkles sacrificial blood on them as the blood of the covenant. Then Moses, Aaron, Nadab, Abihu and seventy elders ascend and see the God of Israel, with the likeness of a pavement of sapphire under God's feet, 'like the very sky for purity,' and they eat and drink. Moses then ascends alone into cloud and fire for forty days.
richContent.didYouKnow: The phrase 'na'aseh v'nishma' — 'we will do and we will hear' — spoken by Israel when ratifying the covenant, became one of the most celebrated lines in all of Torah: acting before fully understanding is seen as the highest form of faith. The Talmud (Shabbat 88a) says that when Israel spoke these words, 600,000 ministering angels came and placed two crowns on each Israelite's head. The laws in this portion also forbid charging interest when lending to the poor (Exodus 22:24), framed not as policy but as divine command.
richContent.historicalContext: The laws of Mishpatim bear close structural similarity to the Code of Hammurabi (c. 1754 BCE), a Babylonian law code that uses the same 'if X then Y' (casuistic) legal format and covers many of the same topics: ox-goring, theft, property damage, slavery. This parallel has long fascinated scholars: do the similarities reflect a shared legal tradition across the ancient Near East, or direct borrowing? Significant differences exist: under Hammurabi's law 8, a livestock thief who could not pay was put to death, while in Exodus a thief who cannot pay is sold to make restitution (22:2).
richContent.jewishTradition: This portion contains the Torah's foundational statement of social ethics, and the rabbis derived from it much of classical Jewish civil law — torts, contracts, property, labor relations. The Talmud (Bava Metzia 59b) cites Rabbi Eliezer's count: the Torah warns against mistreating the stranger in thirty-six places (some say forty-six), and in this portion the reason is spelled out: 'for you know the feelings of the stranger, having yourselves been strangers in the land of Egypt' (23:9).

name: Terumah
summary: God instructs Moses to collect donations from the willing-hearted Israelites to build a portable Tabernacle (Mishkan) as a divine dwelling among the people. Detailed blueprints are given for the Ark of the Covenant with its gold cherubim, the menorah, the table for showbread, and the structure of the Tabernacle itself.

richContent.narrativeSummary: After the dramatic legislation of Mishpatim, with Moses now on the mountain for forty days, God pivots to architecture: the Israelites are to build a portable sanctuary — the Mishkan, the 'dwelling place' — so that God can dwell among them. But the donation is to come only from 'every person whose heart moves them to give' — generosity must be voluntary, not compelled. The blueprint God provides is exquisitely detailed: an Ark of acacia wood overlaid inside and out with pure gold, with a solid gold 'mercy seat' lid flanked by two hammered gold cherubim whose wings spread upward; a golden menorah hammered from a single piece of pure gold with six branches, its cups shaped like almond blossoms; a table of acacia wood with gold molding for the showbread; and the Tabernacle structure itself — curtains of fine linen and blue, purple, and crimson yarn with cherubim woven into them, frames of acacia wood with silver bases, a screen at the entrance. The whole apparatus is designed to be assembled, disassembled, and carried through the desert.
richContent.didYouKnow: The Tabernacle's dimensions and the quantities of materials specified are so precise that scholars and architects have produced detailed reconstruction models of what it would have looked like. The Ark of the Covenant (aron ha-brit) has inspired centuries of search and speculation about its location. The Torah specifies its exact dimensions: 2.5 cubits long, 1.5 cubits wide, 1.5 cubits tall (roughly 45 × 27 × 27 inches). The menorah, beaten from a single piece of gold with almond-blossom shaped cups, was to be made together with its tongs and pans from one talent of pure gold (25:39).
richContent.historicalContext: Portable tent-shrines were not unique to ancient Israel. Egyptian temple reliefs show the military camp of Ramesses II at the battle of Kadesh, and scholars such as Michael Homan compare its layout to the Tabernacle: a courtyard twice as long as it is wide, entered from the east, leading to a reception tent and a square throne tent. The 'Tent of Meeting' concept has parallels in Ugaritic literature and across the ancient Near East. The Tabernacle's inner curtains — blue, purple, and crimson with cherubim woven in — use costly dyes that were also prized in Canaanite and Phoenician luxury textiles. The blue (tekhelet) and purple (argaman) dyes were made from murex sea snails and were extraordinarily expensive.
richContent.jewishTradition: Nachmanides argued that the Tabernacle represents a continuation of Sinai: just as God descended in fire and cloud on the mountain, the cloud would fill the Mishkan. The rabbis read the details symbolically: the Talmud (Yoma 72b) says the Ark was three nested boxes, gold, wood and gold, and learns from the gold inside and out that a Torah scholar's inside must match his outside.

name: Tetzaveh
summary: God commands the Israelites to bring pure olive oil for the eternal lamp of the Tabernacle. Elaborate instructions describe the priestly garments for Aaron and his sons: the ephod, breastplate with twelve gemstones for the twelve tribes, the robe, tunic, and turban. A seven-day ordination ceremony is prescribed for the priests, along with instructions for the golden incense altar.

richContent.narrativeSummary: Moses himself is conspicuously absent from this portion: his name does not appear anywhere in it, the only portion from his birth to the end of Numbers without it, while Aaron and his sons take center stage as the priestly dynasty is established. The priestly garments are works of astonishing craft: an ephod of gold, blue, purple, and crimson thread woven together with two onyx shoulder stones engraved with the names of the twelve tribes; a breastplate of twelve precious gemstones in four rows, each engraved with a tribal name so Aaron carries all Israel over his heart when he enters the sanctuary; a robe of solid blue with a hem of golden bells alternating with colored pomegranates so his approach to God is always announced. A golden plate on the turban is engraved 'Holy to YHWH.' The ordination ceremony takes seven days: Moses slaughters bulls and rams, applies blood to the ear, thumb, and big toe of Aaron and his sons, and sprinkles blood on their garments. The golden incense altar that closes the portion is for incense, burned every morning and evening, not for animal offerings; only once a year is blood put on its horns (30:10).
richContent.didYouKnow: From Moses's birth to the end of Numbers, this is the only parsha in which his name does not appear. The Baal HaTurim connects this to Moses's plea 'erase me from Your book' in the next portion (Ki Tisa), citing the rule that a sage's curse comes true even when it was conditional. The twelve gemstones on the High Priest's breastplate — odem, pitdah, barekat, nofech, sapir, yahalom, leshem, shevo, achlamah, tarshish, shoham, yashfeh — are among the most debated terms in all of Torah: translators disagree on what most of them are, resulting in wildly different English versions.
richContent.historicalContext: Elaborate priestly vestments were common in the ancient Near East: Egyptian priests wore white linen robes and performed purification rituals before approaching temple precincts; Mesopotamian temple priests had specific garments for specific ceremonies. The Urim and Thummim, inserted into the breastplate for divination, appear to have been a form of lot-casting by which God's will was sought, comparable to other ancient Near Eastern oracular devices.
richContent.jewishTradition: The priestly garments were understood by the rabbis as having atoning power corresponding to the sins they covered: the robe, with its ringing bells, atoned for malicious speech, a sound atoning for a sound; the breastplate of judgment atoned for improper judgments; the turban for arrogance; the tunic for bloodshed (Arakhin 16a). After the Temple's destruction, prayer was understood to replace sacrifice, and one opinion in the Talmud (Berakhot 26b) holds that the daily prayers were instituted to correspond to the daily Temple offerings. Kohanim (priests) still bless the congregation during synagogue services today, a direct continuation of the priestly role.

name: Ki Tisa
summary: While Moses is on the mountain, the Israelites panic and pressure Aaron into making a Golden Calf to worship. God threatens to destroy the people; Moses pleads for them and descends, smashing the tablets in fury. He destroys the calf; the Levites kill about three thousand people, and God strikes the people with a plague. Moses returns to God and pleads again for forgiveness; God relents and renews the covenant. Moses descends with new tablets, his face radiating divine light.

richContent.narrativeSummary: Moses is so long in coming down from the mountain that the people below crack: 'Make us a god,' they tell Aaron, 'for this Moses — we don't know what became of him.' Aaron collects their gold earrings, melts them, and fashions a calf, and when the people proclaim 'These are your gods, Israel, who brought you out of Egypt,' Aaron builds an altar and announces a festival. On the mountain God tells Moses what's happening and proposes erasing the nation and starting over with Moses — 'I'll make you a great nation' — and Moses talks God out of it with three arguments: reputation (what will Egypt say?), mercy, and the covenant with the patriarchs. He descends carrying the tablets, sees the dancing, and in a fury smashes them at the foot of the mountain. He grinds the calf to powder, scatters it on water, and makes the people drink it. In the aftermath, the tribe of Levi rallies to Moses and kills about three thousand people. Moses then ascends again for forty more days to plead for forgiveness, entering an extraordinary negotiation in which God reveals the divine attributes of mercy: 'YHWH, YHWH, God, compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in kindness and truth.' The covenant is renewed, and Moses descends with new tablets, his face shining with divine light so intensely he must wear a veil.
richContent.didYouKnow: Moses's shattering of the tablets is one of the Torah's most daring acts — destroying the physical words of God in an act of fury — and the Midrash (Shemot Rabbah 43:1) justifies it with a parable: when a prince's bride was unfaithful before the wedding, his agent tore up the marriage contract, saying it was better that she be judged as a single woman than as a married one. The thirteen divine attributes of mercy enumerated in this portion ('YHWH, YHWH, God compassionate and gracious...') became the centerpiece of the Yom Kippur liturgy, repeated over and over as the central plea for forgiveness. Moses's shining face is rendered in Latin as 'cornuta' (horned) due to a translation ambiguity, which is why Michelangelo's famous sculpture of Moses has horns.
richContent.historicalContext: Bull or calf imagery was ubiquitous in ancient Canaanite and broader Near Eastern religion. The storm-god Baal was regularly depicted standing on a bull, and the golden calf may represent not a replacement for God but a pedestal or vehicle for the divine — a misapplication of surrounding religious iconography to YHWH worship. The book of Kings says that Jeroboam (10th century BCE) set up golden calves at Dan and Bethel with almost the same words used here: 'This is your god, O Israel, who brought you up from the land of Egypt' (1 Kings 12:28). Scholars debate which account shaped the other. At Tel Dan, archaeologists have uncovered a sacred compound with a large horned altar, but no golden calf has been found.
richContent.jewishTradition: Ki Tisa contains the Torah's most dramatic moment of divine-human negotiation, and Moses's intercessory arguments became the model for rabbinic prayer theology: God can be argued with, can be appealed to through logic and precedent, and — crucially — can change course. The sin of the golden calf haunts the entire tradition: the Talmud (Sanhedrin 102a) says that every punishment that comes to the world contains a small share of the punishment for the golden calf. Yet the portion also contains the most generous description of divine mercy in the entire Torah — the Thirteen Attributes — making it a portrait of both the depths of failure and the heights of forgiveness.

name: Vayakhel
summary: Moses gathers the entire community of Israel, reiterates the Sabbath commandment, and calls for donations to build the Tabernacle. The people respond with overwhelming generosity. The master craftsmen Bezalel and Oholiab, filled with divine spirit and skill, lead the construction of the Tabernacle and all its furnishings.

richContent.narrativeSummary: After the golden calf catastrophe and Moses's successful intercession, the community reassembles — 'vayakhel,' he gathered — for a fresh start. Moses's very first instruction is Shabbat: even for the sacred work of building God's sanctuary, no fire shall be kindled on the seventh day. Then comes the call for donations, and the response is extraordinary: morning after morning the people bring gold, silver, copper, fine fabrics, skins, acacia wood, spices, oil, and precious stones — so much that the craftsmen tell Moses the people are bringing more than is needed, and Moses has it announced through the camp that they should stop. The architects of the entire project are two men: Bezalel of the tribe of Judah, 'filled with the spirit of God' in wisdom, understanding, and knowledge in all craftsmanship; and Oholiab of the tribe of Dan. Together they lead teams of skilled artisans in fabricating every element of the Tabernacle — the curtains, the frames, the screens, the Ark, the menorah, the altars — all executed to the specifications God gave Moses on the mountain.
richContent.didYouKnow: The juxtaposition of Shabbat before Tabernacle construction has been read by the rabbis as the Torah's method of defining what 'work' means: the 39 categories of creative labor prohibited on Shabbat are derived from the 39 types of work performed to build the Tabernacle. Bezalel's name can be read 'in the shadow of God' (be-tzel El), a pun the Talmud itself makes (Berakhot 55a), and the same page says Bezalel 'knew how to join the letters with which heaven and earth were created.'
richContent.historicalContext: The sheer quantity of precious materials described in the Tabernacle donations — tons of gold, silver, and copper — has led some scholars to argue that the text reflects idealized temple-building propaganda rather than desert reality. Others note that the spoils taken from Egypt at the Exodus ('they despoiled Egypt,' Exodus 12:36) could plausibly account for significant gold reserves. Other ancient Near Eastern texts also describe temples built to a divine plan: in the Sumerian Gudea Cylinders (c. 2125 BCE), Gudea, ruler of Lagash, sees the plan of the god Ningirsu's temple drawn on a lapis lazuli tablet in a dream, and then builds it.
richContent.jewishTradition: The placing of the Sabbath commandment immediately before the Tabernacle construction work is the rabbis' textual basis for defining the thirty-nine major categories of prohibited Shabbat labor (the 'melachot') — each derived from an activity performed by the Tabernacle craftsmen. This Talmudic derivation (Shabbat 49b) is one of the most elaborate examples of rabbinic legal reasoning and is the foundation of all Orthodox Shabbat law. The overwhelming generosity of the donors — giving until they were told to stop — became the ideal for communal fundraising in Jewish communities for millennia: a willing heart, not a compelled hand.

name: Pekudei
summary: The Tabernacle construction is completed and Moses accounts for all the gold, silver, and copper donated. The priestly garments are finished and Moses blesses the craftsmen. On the first day of the first month, Moses erects the Tabernacle, anoints and consecrates it, and the cloud of God's glory fills it — guiding the Israelites in all their travels.

richContent.narrativeSummary: Pekudei opens with a meticulous accounting of all donated materials — every ounce of gold, silver, and copper is tallied, and the purposes to which each was applied are listed. The Midrash (Shemot Rabbah 51:6) says Moses gave this accounting because some people whispered that he had grown rich from the donations. The priestly garments are completed exactly as commanded, and the Torah's repeated phrase 'as YHWH commanded Moses' echoes seven times through the account of the garments like a refrain, emphasizing obedience as the measure of holiness. Then on the first day of the first month of the second year, Moses alone erects the entire Tabernacle — a kind of priestly ritual in which each element is anointed and consecrated as it is placed. Aaron and his sons are dressed in their garments and anointed. The book of Exodus ends in a blaze of divine glory: the cloud of God descends on the Tabernacle so powerfully that even Moses cannot enter. From this point on, the cloud over the Tabernacle by day and fire by night will guide every movement of the Israelite camp — when it lifts, they travel; when it settles, they rest.
richContent.didYouKnow: The book of Exodus ends with Moses unable to enter the completed Tabernacle because God's glory filled it so completely — yet in the next book (Leviticus), God calls to Moses from within the Tabernacle. The rabbis explain that Moses was temporarily excluded by the overwhelming intensity of divine presence, but that God then called him in with a voice calibrated only for his ears, so the other Israelites heard nothing. The phrase 'as YHWH commanded Moses' appears eighteen times in this account of the construction, and the Jerusalem Talmud (Berakhot 4:3) connects these eighteen mentions to the eighteen blessings of the Amidah prayer.
richContent.historicalContext: The accounting of materials in Pekudei has parallels in ancient Near Eastern temple construction records. Egyptian papyri and Mesopotamian administrative texts from the second millennium document elaborate inventories of temple goods, tracking every ingot of precious metal and bolt of cloth donated or expended. The transparency of the accounting — publicly announced and verified — reflects a genuine ancient practice of temple stewardship, where priests were obligated to account for divine property and demonstrate that nothing was diverted to private use.
richContent.jewishTradition: The completion of the Tabernacle is seen in Jewish tradition as a moment of cosmic repair: the Midrash (Tanchuma Pekudei 2) says the Tabernacle is equal to the creation of the world, matching its parts to the days of creation — the curtains to the heavens, the dividing veil to the firmament, the laver's water to the gathered waters, the menorah to the lights in the sky, the cherubim's spread wings to the birds, and the high priest to the first human. The cloud of divine glory that fills the Tabernacle is the same cloud that appeared at Sinai and will appear again at the Temple's dedication under Solomon, creating a thread of divine presence across Israel's entire history. When the work is done, Moses blesses those who did it (39:43); Rashi says the blessing was 'May it be the will of God that His Shechinah rest upon the work of your hands.'

name: Vayikra
summary: God calls to Moses from the Tabernacle and begins dictating the laws of sacrifice. The different types of offerings are detailed: burnt offerings of cattle, sheep, or birds; grain offerings; peace offerings; sin offerings for unintentional violations by priests, leaders, and ordinary people; and guilt offerings for specific wrongs.

richContent.narrativeSummary: Leviticus opens with 'Vayikra', 'He called': God calls to Moses from the Tent of Meeting. By scribal tradition, the word's last letter, aleph, is written small in the Torah scroll. What follows is an ordered set of laws for offerings, some given freely and some required after a wrong. The burnt offering (olah) is burned whole on the altar; no one eats any of it, though the priest keeps the hide (7:8). The grain offering (minchah) is usually choice flour with oil and frankincense. The well-being offering (shelamim) comes from the herd or the flock; its fat is burned on the altar, and next week's portion gives the rest to the priest and the one who brought it (7:15–34). Purgation offerings (chatat), mostly for wrongs done by mistake, depend on who did wrong: a bull for the anointed priest or the whole community, a male goat for a chieftain, a female goat or sheep for anyone else. For a few cases (5:1–4) there is a sliding scale: someone who cannot afford a ewe or she-goat may bring two turtledoves or two pigeons, and someone who cannot afford those, a tenth of an ephah of choice flour. The guilt offering (asham) covers, among other cases, misusing holy things by mistake, and cheating someone and swearing falsely about it; the wrongdoer also pays back what was taken, plus a fifth.
richContent.didYouKnow: The opening word, Vayikra, is written in the Torah scroll with a small aleph. The Kitzur Baal HaTurim says Moses wanted to write 'vayikar' ('happened upon'), the word used for God appearing to Balaam (Numbers 23:4), but God told him to include the aleph, so Moses wrote it small. Rashi, commenting on the word itself rather than the small letter, calls 'vayikra' a word of affection. Leviticus is also called Torat Kohanim, 'the teaching of the priests'. In a midrash (Vayikra Rabbah 7:3), Rabbi Asi asks why children begin learning Torah with Leviticus, not Genesis, and answers: 'the children are pure and the offerings are pure; let the pure come and engage in the pure.'
richContent.historicalContext: Offerings to the gods were part of worship across the ancient Near East. Ritual texts from the city of Ugarit on the Syrian coast, written before it was destroyed in the early 12th century BCE, name offerings with words related to those in Leviticus, such as šlmm (compare shelamim, the well-being offering), though they list what was offered more than they explain what the rites meant. Much earlier, around 2000 BCE, Mesopotamian officials recorded thousands of sheep, goats and cattle delivered to temples. Leviticus sets out its offerings in order, varies some by who brings them, and lets people bring less when they cannot afford more (5:7–13). When this happened is debated. Scholars who date the Exodus usually place it in the 13th century BCE, and many doubt it can be dated; traditional Jewish chronology puts the Exodus in the year 2448 (c. 1313 BCE), and the Tabernacle was set up on the first day of the first month of the second year (Exodus 40:17).
richContent.jewishTradition: After the Temple was destroyed in 70 CE, offerings could no longer be brought, and the rabbis taught that prayer and Torah study stand in their place. The Talmud (Berakhot 26b) gives two views of where the three daily prayers come from: one traces them to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob; the other to the Temple offerings, with the evening prayer matching the parts left burning on the altar through the night. The same view links the Musaf prayer, added on Shabbat, festivals and the New Moon, to the additional offering brought on those days (Numbers 28–29). In the Talmud (Menachot 110a), Rabbi Yitzchak says that anyone who studies the law of the purgation offering (chatat, often translated 'sin offering') is credited as though he had brought one, and the same for the guilt offering.

name: Tzav
summary: God gives Moses detailed instructions for the priests on how to perform and eat from the various sacrifices: the burnt offering, grain offering, sin offering, guilt offering, and peace offering. The prohibition on eating fat or blood is reiterated. Moses then performs the ordination ceremony for Aaron and his sons, anointing them and consecrating them over seven days.

richContent.narrativeSummary: Where Vayikra addressed the Israelites as donors of sacrifices, Tzav addresses the priests as the people who handle them — the professional liturgical specialists whose work must be done with precision and reverence. The burnt offering's fire must never be extinguished; the priest must remove the ashes in his linen vestments each morning and carry them outside the camp in his regular clothes — a humble, unglamorous task that opens the day of divine service. The grain offering belongs to Aaron and his sons, but the High Priest's own personal grain offering must be burned entirely — he cannot eat from it. The ban on eating fat and blood is repeated: no fat of ox, sheep or goat, and no blood of bird or animal 'in any of your settlements' (7:23–27), so it applies wherever Israelites live. The ordination of Aaron and his sons unfolds with ceremonial precision over seven days: each day Moses slaughters animals, burns portions on the altar, applies blood to Aaron's right ear, right thumb, and right big toe, sprinkles blood on the altar and garments — and Aaron must not leave the Tabernacle entrance for the full week.
richContent.didYouKnow: The blood put on the right ear, right thumb and right big toe of the priests at their ordination (8:23–24) is put on the same three places on a person healed of tzara'at, a skin affliction, later in this book (14:14). The anointed priest's own grain offering, half in the morning and half in the evening, is burned whole and not eaten (6:13–16). Maimonides (Guide 3:46) explains that if a priest offered his own grain offering and then ate it, it would look as if no service had been done.
richContent.historicalContext: A text from Emar in Syria, from about 1250 BCE (Emar 369), describes the installation of a high priestess, with anointing and seven days of daily sacrifices. Scholars compare it with the ordination in Leviticus 8. The Torah does not explain why blood is put on the right ear, thumb and big toe; later commentators, such as Rabbeinu Bahya, offered symbolic readings.
richContent.jewishTradition: The ban on blood, 'you must not consume any blood… in any of your settlements' (7:26), is the basis of the Jewish practice of salting and rinsing meat (melichah) to draw out the blood before cooking. The Torah itself gives the reason later in Leviticus: 'the life of the flesh is in the blood,' and blood is set aside for the altar to make atonement (17:11, 14).
